items.prompt: A partition call begins at index start in a string of length n. Which exclusive end boundaries produce non-empty next segments?

options.text: start + 1 through n, inclusive.
start through n - 1.
0 through start.
Only n.

feedback.reason: A non-empty segment [start, end) needs end > start and may extend to the input end.

blocks.text: Enumerate every nonempty prefix of the unresolved suffix
A half-open segment [start, end) contains end - start elements. Nonemptiness therefore requires end > start, making start + 1 the smallest candidate end.

The exclusive end may equal n, which selects the whole remaining suffix. Enumerating every integer end from start + 1 through n covers every nonempty prefix exactly once before the segment predicate filters candidates.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: end = start creates an empty segment and end = n must be available. These boundaries overlap or precede the unresolved suffix. This omits shorter first segments.

blocks.title: Boundary interval
blocks.text: For 0 <= start < n, legal nonempty candidate ends are exactly start + 1, ..., n.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.start_to_n_minus_one: end = start creates an empty segment and end = n must be available.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.zero_to_start: These boundaries overlap or precede the unresolved suffix.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.only_n: Choosing only n considers the entire suffix but omits every shorter valid prefix and every multi-segment continuation.

items.prompt: When is a full segmentation complete?

options.text: When the next unresolved start index equals n.
When at least one segment has been chosen.
When a chosen end is less than n.
When the latest segment has length one.

feedback.reason: Completion means the chosen segments cover the input exactly with no gap or remainder.

blocks.text: The next unresolved index measures coverage
Each accepted segment starts at the current unresolved index and passes its exclusive end to the child. This invariant makes the path cover exactly [0, start) without gaps or overlaps.

When start == n, the covered prefix is [0, n), which is the whole input, and no suffix remains. A nonempty path, a length-one last segment, or an end below n does not by itself establish total coverage.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: A non-empty path may leave input uncovered. That means a suffix remains. Segment length does not define total coverage.

blocks.title: Completion invariant
blocks.text: Record a partition only when the unresolved boundary reaches n.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.path_nonempty: One or more valid segments may cover only a prefix, leaving an unresolved suffix.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.end_less_n: An exclusive end below n means positions [end, n) remain unprocessed.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.segment_length_one: The latest segment's length says nothing about whether earlier segments collectively reached the input end.

items.prompt: Why are empty segments usually excluded from ordinary partition enumeration?

options.text: Choosing end = start makes no input progress and can cause infinite recursion or duplicate decompositions.
An empty segment can never be valid in any contract.
Exclusive indices cannot represent empty ranges.
Empty segments prevent sorting.

feedback.reason: Every recursive choice should advance the unresolved boundary unless the contract explicitly models empty components.

blocks.text: A recursive segment choice must make progress
Choosing end = start forms the valid half-open empty range [start, start), but the child receives the same start value as its parent. No input is consumed.

If the same empty choice remains available, recursion can repeat the identical state indefinitely. Even with an artificial stop, inserting empty segments in many positions creates duplicate decompositions. Ordinary partition contracts therefore require end > start; specialized contracts must define separate progress controls.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: Some specialized contracts may allow it; the issue is the ordinary non-empty partition model. A half-open range [start, start) represents an empty segment. Sorting is unrelated.

blocks.title: Progress rule
blocks.text: A child boundary must be strictly later unless the contract explicitly models emptiness with another decreasing measure.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.empty_never_valid: Some specialized contracts may allow it; the issue is the ordinary non-empty partition model.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.indices_forbidden: A half-open range [start, start) represents an empty segment.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorting_needed: Sorting changes element order and is unrelated to whether a boundary advances or repeats the same recursive state.

items.prompt: A palindrome-partition solver considers substring [start, end). When should it recurse from end?

options.text: Only if the chosen substring satisfies the palindrome predicate.
For every possible boundary, even when the segment is invalid.
Only for one-character segments.
Only when end equals n.

feedback.reason: Segment validity is part of candidate legality.

blocks.text: Validate the fixed segment before entering its suffix
The candidate end fixes substring [start, end) permanently in this branch. If it is not a palindrome, every descendant partition would retain that invalid segment.

Only after the predicate accepts the segment should it be appended and recursion continue from end. Length one is sufficient but not necessary for palindromicity, and end need not equal n because valid intermediate segments lead to multi-part results.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: An invalid fixed segment cannot become valid later. Longer palindromes are also legal. Intermediate segments are necessary for multi-part partitions.

blocks.title: Fixed-prefix rule
blocks.text: Recurse from end only when the segment permanently added to the prefix satisfies the required predicate.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.always: An invalid fixed segment cannot become valid later.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.only_if_length_one: Longer strings such as "aba" are palindromes and must remain legal segment choices.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.only_at_n: A valid intermediate segment ending before n is necessary to construct any partition with multiple segments.

items.prompt: After recursively exploring a chosen segment, what must happen before trying another end boundary?

options.text: Remove the segment from the current partition path.
Delete the segment from the original string.
Clear all completed partitions.
Reset start to zero.

feedback.reason: The current path is branch-local state and must return to the parent partition prefix.

blocks.text: Restore the parent partition prefix
Appending [start, end) changes the shared live path only for that child branch. After recursion returns, the parent loop will try another end from the same start.

Popping the chosen segment restores the exact parent prefix before the next sibling. The immutable input and previously stored result snapshots must remain intact, and the parent's start is not reset because its loop is still enumerating prefixes of the same unresolved suffix.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: The input remains shared and immutable. Sibling results remain valid. The parent start remains unchanged while its loop tries another end.

blocks.title: Sibling invariant
blocks.text: Every candidate end at one depth is evaluated from the same restored partition prefix.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.delete_input: The source string remains shared and immutable; deleting characters would change every later boundary and branch.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.clear_results: Completed partitions found by the child are durable output snapshots and must not be erased during branch restoration.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.reset_start_zero: The parent start remains unchanged while its loop tries another end.

items.prompt: Which relation between consecutive segments prevents gaps and overlaps?

options.text: The next segment starts exactly at the previous segment's exclusive end.
Every segment starts at zero.
The next segment starts one position after the previous exclusive end.
The next segment may begin at any index.

feedback.reason: Exact boundary handoff makes the segments contiguous and collectively covering.

blocks.text: Half-open segments meet at one shared boundary
If one segment is [a, b), it contains indices a through b - 1. The next segment must start at b: [b, c) then begins with the first still-uncovered index.
Starting again at zero overlaps the covered prefix. Starting at b + 1 skips index b because b was excluded from the previous segment. An arbitrary start provides no coverage guarantee.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: That overlaps earlier segments. That leaves a one-position gap. Arbitrary starts can create gaps and overlaps.

blocks.title: Composition identity
blocks.text: [a, b) followed by [b, c) covers [a, c) exactly once.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.next_start_zero: Restarting at zero reprocesses the already covered prefix and overlaps earlier segments.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.next_start_end_plus_one: Because the exclusive end itself was not covered, starting at end + 1 leaves index end in a one-position gap.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.arbitrary_start: A start below end overlaps covered input, while a start above end leaves a gap; only equality guarantees contiguity.

items.prompt: A solver records a partition as soon as the latest segment is valid, even though unprocessed input remains. What defect results?

options.text: It records incomplete partitions that do not cover the full input.
It automatically removes duplicate partitions.
It changes auxiliary space to O(1).
It sorts all segments.

feedback.reason: Local segment validity is not the full result contract.

blocks.text: Local validity does not imply complete coverage
A valid segment proves only that one component satisfies its predicate. If its exclusive end is below n, positions [end, n) remain uncovered.

Recording at this point emits a partial prefix as if it were a full partition. The snapshot should instead be recorded by the base case start == n, after every input position belongs to exactly one valid segment.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: The defect is incomplete coverage. Recording timing does not remove path state. No sorting occurs.

blocks.title: Result boundary
blocks.text: Segment validity authorizes recursion; full coverage authorizes output.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.duplicate_control: Premature recording adds incomplete outputs; it does not compare or remove duplicate partitions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.constant_space: The recursive path and snapshots still consume space, so recording timing cannot make auxiliary space constant.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorted_segments: No comparison or reordering occurs; the defect concerns incomplete input coverage.

items.prompt: For the string "abc", how many possible cut locations exist between characters?

feedback.reason: A length-n sequence has n - 1 internal boundaries where a cut may be present or absent.

blocks.text: Cuts live in gaps, not on characters
The three characters occupy positions a, b, and c. Optional cuts can occur only in the two internal gaps: a|b and b|c.

The outer boundaries before a and after c delimit the whole string; they are not optional internal cut decisions. Thus a length-three string has 3 - 1 = 2 cut locations. Choosing cut or no cut independently at each gap later yields 2^2 partitions.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: There are three characters but only two internal gaps. Both gaps between a-b and b-c are possible cut locations. Boundaries at the outer ends do not represent optional internal cuts.

blocks.title: Counting rule
blocks.text: n elements create n - 1 internal adjacency gaps.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.three: There are three characters but only two internal gaps.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one: Both gaps between a-b and b-c are possible cut locations.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.four: Boundaries at the outer ends do not represent optional internal cuts.

items.prompt: When is choosing the entire remaining suffix as one segment legal?

options.text: When [start, n) satisfies the segment predicate.
Always, regardless of segment constraints.
Never; partitions must contain at least two segments.
Only when the suffix is empty.

feedback.reason: The boundary end = n is a normal candidate representing one final segment.

blocks.text: The whole suffix is the candidate end = n
For start < n, choosing end = n forms the nonempty segment [start, n). It is evaluated by exactly the same predicate as every shorter candidate.

If valid, appending it and recursing from n reaches the completion base case, so it may finish either a one-segment partition or a longer prefix. If invalid, the boundary is rejected; the empty suffix at start == n is completion, not another ordinary segment.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: The segment must satisfy the same validity contract as shorter choices. A one-segment partition can be valid. The empty suffix is completion, not an ordinary non-empty segment.

blocks.title: Final-segment rule
blocks.text: Allow end = n, but require [start, n) to satisfy the same segment predicate.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.always: The segment must satisfy the same validity contract as shorter choices.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.never: When the entire suffix satisfies the predicate, it is a legal final segment and may form a one-segment partition.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.only_empty: The empty suffix is completion, not an ordinary non-empty segment.

items.prompt: Which conditions make [start, end) a legal next partition segment? Select all that apply.

options.text: end is greater than start.
end is at most the input length.
The segment satisfies the required predicate.
start is reset to zero for every segment.

feedback.reason: A legal segment advances the boundary, stays inside the input, and satisfies the segment contract.

blocks.text: A legal segment advances, stays in bounds, and passes its predicate

items: end > start makes [start, end) nonempty and guarantees recursive progress.
end <= n keeps the exclusive endpoint inside the input slicing range.
The segment predicate must accept [start, end), because that fixed component remains in every descendant.

blocks.text: After all checks pass, the child receives start = end, continuing at the first unresolved index. Resetting start to zero would overlap every segment with the already covered prefix.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: The parent prefix already covers [0, start). Resetting to zero makes the next segment reprocess that region instead of extending coverage.

blocks.title: Candidate contract
blocks.text: Require start < end <= n, predicate validity, and child start = end.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.start_reset_zero: The current prefix already covers input before start, so resetting to zero overlaps processed positions and breaks contiguous forward coverage.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.end_greater_start: The segment length is end - start, so strict inequality makes it positive and advances recursion.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.end_at_most_n: An exclusive end may equal n but cannot exceed it without slicing beyond the input.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.predicate_valid: The chosen segment is permanently included in this branch, so it must already satisfy the result's segment rule.

items.prompt: Which tests are important for partition-boundary correctness? Select all that apply.

options.text: Empty input under an explicitly defined empty-partition contract.
A one-element input.
An input where both the whole sequence and a multi-segment split are valid.
Only one long random input.

feedback.reason: Boundary review needs identity, minimum non-empty, and competing-cut cases.

blocks.text: Test the identity, minimum size, and competing boundaries

items: Empty input tests the explicitly declared identity: whether one empty partition is a completed result.
One element tests the smallest nonempty segment and end = n without any internal cut.
An input with both whole and split solutions tests that end = n and shorter sibling boundaries are all retained.

blocks.text: These cases isolate start == n, start + 1, and competing ends. One long random input may cover them accidentally but cannot identify which off-by-one or restoration rule failed.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: A single long random case has weak diagnostic power and may miss the empty identity, one-element boundary, or coexistence of whole and split results.

blocks.title: Boundary matrix
blocks.text: Test start == n, end == start + 1, end == n, and multiple valid sibling ends.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.only_long_random: One random case may not exercise or isolate the exact empty, one-element, and end-equality boundaries where off-by-one defects occur.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.single_element: It should have one possible non-empty segment.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.whole_and_split: It verifies end = n and shorter boundaries.

items.prompt: Which conditions can soundly prune a partition branch? Select all that apply.

options.text: The newly chosen segment violates a mandatory predicate.
The path already exceeds a hard maximum segment count.
The remaining length cannot satisfy a hard minimum size for the required remaining segments.
The segment looks unusual but satisfies every stated constraint.

feedback.reason: Partition pruning follows from fixed-segment validity and explicit capacity constraints.

blocks.text: Prune only on a permanent violation or impossible capacity

items: An invalid fixed segment remains in every descendant, so later suffix choices cannot repair it.
Once a hard maximum segment count is exceeded, adding more segments cannot reduce the count.
If remaining input is shorter than the minimum total length required by remaining slots, supply cannot meet demand.

blocks.text: Each accepted rule proves failure for every completion. A segment that merely looks unusual but satisfies all constraints may still lead to a valid partition and can at most be ordered later.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: Subjective appearance supplies no invariant or bound. Removing a legal-looking-unusual segment can make enumeration incomplete.

blocks.title: Pruning rule
blocks.text: Omit a partition branch only when its fixed prefix is invalid or its remaining capacity is provably insufficient.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.segment_looks_unusual: An unusual but contract-valid segment may still begin a valid completion; preference can change order but cannot justify omission.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.invalid_fixed_segment: The segment is already fixed in the prefix, and later boundaries affect only the suffix, so no descendant can repair it.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.too_many_segments: Every continuation can only retain or increase the current segment count, never bring it back below the hard maximum.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.insufficient_remaining_length: The branch has less remaining material than the mandatory minimum demand of its remaining segment slots.

elements.text: If start equals n, record a snapshot of the current partition and return.
Enumerate exclusive end boundaries from start + 1 through n.
Check whether [start, end) is a legal segment.
Append the segment, recurse from end, then pop it.

feedback.reason: Completion is resolved before generating segments, and only valid segments become child branches.

blocks.text: Resolve completion before enumerating the next segment

items: If start == n, record a detached snapshot of the current partition and return; no unresolved suffix remains.
Otherwise enumerate end from start + 1 through n.
For each end, validate the fixed candidate [start, end).
Append a valid segment, recurse from end, then pop it before the next sibling end.

blocks.text: Returning at the base case prevents generation of an empty extra segment. Validation before append keeps invalid components out of the path, while pop restores the same parent prefix for every candidate end.

blocks.title: Why this order matters
blocks.text: The order follows causal dependencies: If start equals n, record a snapshot of the current partition. Then Enumerate exclusive end boundaries from start + 1 through n. Then Check whether [start, end) is a legal segment. Then Append the segment, recurse from end, then pop it. Reversing a dependency either evaluates an unprepared state or leaves branch state unrecovered.

blocks.title: Call contract
blocks.text: At start, either record-and-return at n or enumerate nonempty valid prefixes of [start, n).

items.prompt: Arrange the operations for one chosen partition boundary.

elements.text: Append the valid segment to the path.
Recurse from end, then remove the segment.

feedback.reason: The boundary defines a candidate segment whose legality is checked before mutation.

blocks.text: One boundary becomes one reversible branch

items: Form or reference [start, end), the exact segment defined by this boundary.
Evaluate the mandatory segment predicate.
Append only a valid segment to the live partition path.
Recurse from end, then pop so another end is tested from the same prefix.

blocks.text: The predicate needs a defined range, recursion needs the appended segment, and the next sibling needs its removal. Reordering any of these dependencies admits invalid state or contaminates sibling paths.

blocks.title: Why this order matters
blocks.text: The order follows causal dependencies: Identify the segment [start, end). Then Evaluate the required segment predicate. Then Append the valid segment to the path. Then Recurse from end, then remove the segment. Reversing a dependency either evaluates an unprepared state or leaves branch state unrecovered.

blocks.title: Branch invariant
blocks.text: A segment enters the path only after validation and leaves it before the next boundary.

items.prompt: Arrange the completion flow when the final chosen segment reaches n.

elements.text: Record a snapshot at the completion base case.
Return and remove the final segment from the live path.

feedback.reason: The final segment becomes part of the completed path before the base case records it.

blocks.text: The base case must see the final segment

items: Append the valid segment [start, n) to the live path.
Recurse with start = n.
The base case records a detached snapshot containing that final segment.
After return, pop the live final segment to restore the parent prefix.

blocks.text: Recording before append omits the final segment. Popping before snapshot has the same defect. Popping afterward changes only the live path; the detached completed partition remains stored.

blocks.title: Why this order matters
blocks.text: The order follows causal dependencies: Append the valid final segment. Then Recurse with start = n. Then Record a snapshot at the completion base case. Then Return and remove the final segment from the live path. Reversing a dependency either evaluates an unprepared state or leaves branch state unrecovered.

blocks.title: Snapshot rule
blocks.text: Complete the live path, snapshot it at start == n, then restore the live path.

items.prompt: A branch must still create r segments, each of length at least m. Arrange the reasoning for a minimum-segment-length capacity prune.

elements.text: If remaining length is smaller than required length, prune.
Otherwise continue with legal boundary choices.

feedback.reason: The branch is impossible when remaining material cannot satisfy mandatory segment sizes.

blocks.text: Compare remaining material with minimum demand

items: Compute remaining = n - start, the number of unprocessed elements.
Compute required = r · m for r remaining segment slots with minimum length m.
If remaining < required, prune because no allocation can meet every minimum.
Otherwise continue legal boundary enumeration; sufficient total length does not guarantee validity.

blocks.text: The inequality is a necessary-capacity test. Equality may be feasible by giving exactly m elements to each slot, so it must not be pruned. Predicate constraints can still make a capacity-feasible branch fail later.

blocks.title: Why this order matters
blocks.text: The order follows causal dependencies: Compute the unprocessed input length. Then Compute the minimum total length required by the remaining segment slots. Then If remaining length is smaller than required length, prune. Then Otherwise continue with legal boundary choices. Reversing a dependency either evaluates an unprepared state or leaves branch state unrecovered.

blocks.title: Capacity formula
blocks.text: Prune exactly when n - start < r · m.

items.prompt: A length-n sequence may be cut or not cut at each internal boundary, and every resulting segment is considered valid. Select the number of complete partitions and maximum recursion depth.
constraints: There are n - 1 internal cut positions.
Each recursive segment consumes at least one element.

feedback.reason: Each internal boundary independently separates or joins adjacent elements.

blocks.text: Each internal gap contributes one binary choice
A length-n sequence has n - 1 gaps between adjacent elements. At each gap, independently choose cut or no cut; each binary decision vector defines exactly one complete contiguous partition.
Multiplying two choices across n - 1 gaps yields exactly 2^(n - 1) partitions, represented by the available O(2^(n-1)) answer. Because every segment is valid, none of these leaves is pruned.
The deepest route cuts every gap and produces n single-element segments, one recursive segment per level. Maximum recursion depth is therefore O(n), not exponential.

blocks.title: Check each dimension independently
blocks.text: O(n!) models order permutations, but a partition preserves input order. The exponential number of leaves does not imply an exponential number of simultaneous frames.

blocks.title: Partition-count rule
blocks.text: Contiguous order-preserving partitions correspond one-to-one with subsets of the n - 1 internal gaps.

items.prompt: A collect-all partition solver returns s partitions, and each partition contains at most n segment references or copied segments. Select a standard upper bound on materialized output work and output space.
constraints: Every returned partition is stored independently.

feedback.reason: Returning s partitions of size up to n is inherently output-sensitive.

blocks.text: Bound the retained output by partitions times maximum size
The solver retains s independent partitions. Under the stated maximum, each stores at most n segment references or copied segment entries, so each output takes O(n) representation work and space.

Multiplying gives the standard upper bounds O(sn) for materialization work and O(sn) for final output space. This is not a universal lower bound because a partition may contain fewer than n stored entries; the prompt now asks for the correct upper bound.

Pruning can reduce invalid search overhead but cannot change how many valid outputs the contract requires. A stronger Θ(sn) claim would need every returned representation to have size proportional to n, which is not assumed here.

blocks.title: Check each dimension independently
blocks.text: O(s) ignores per-partition entries, and O(n) ignores the number of retained partitions. Search stack space is a separate auxiliary quantity.

blocks.title: Output accounting
blocks.text: For s outputs of size at most n, materialized work and retained space are each O(sn).
